modern.text: An automatic watch has no battery, yet it turns random wrist shakes into eight exact beats every second, twenty-eight thousand eight hundred beats an hour, and keeps running for forty-two hours off the wrist.

Chapter one follows how wrist motion enters the watch. Six stacked layers share one 25.6 millimetre plate on ruby bearings: the oscillating rotor and reversing wheels on top, chamfered bridges below, then the escapement and balance wheel above the mainspring barrel and going train.

Whenever your wrist tilts, gravity swings the weighted semicircular rotor on its central ball-bearing hub. Because a wrist moves in every direction, the rotor swings both clockwise and counter-clockwise.

Between the rotor pinion and barrel ratchet sit twin reversing click wheels. They catch opposite swing directions so every motion winds the mainspring barrel one way only through a one hundred and twenty to one reduction, taking eight hundred and forty rotor turns from empty to full.
Chapter two follows how energy is stored. Winding coils the alloy mainspring inside its seventy-two-tooth barrel. seven usable turns deliver six hours each, storing forty-two hours of power.
At full wind, the slipping bridle pressed against the smooth inner wall of the barrel lets the outer coil slide safely at 7.2 newton millimetres, so continued wrist motion can never snap the spring.

As the mainspring unwinds, its flat torque plateau keeps the balance wheel swinging near two hundred and ninety degrees until nearly empty, dropping below two hundred and twenty degrees only near 3.6 newton millimetres. Normal desk wear adds 2.4 hours of reserve each hour, while sedentary wear drains it.

Chapter three traces the four geared stages that multiply speed. First, the mainspring barrel drives the center wheel at six to one, pacing the barrel at one turn every six hours while the center wheel turns once an hour for the minute hand.

Next, the center wheel drives the third wheel at eight to one, and the third wheel drives the fourth wheel at 7.5 to one. Together that is sixty to one, turning the fourth wheel and its blued sweep second hand once every minute.

Finally, the fourth wheel drives the escape pinion at sixteen to one, turning the escape wheel sixteen turns a minute and completing a five thousand seven hundred and sixty to one train from barrel to beat.

Chapter four slows down the Swiss lever escapement that meters time. While the balance swings freely, a ruby stone on the pallet fork locks the fifteen-tooth escape wheel still. As the balance returns, its roller impulse jewel enters the fork notch and unlocks the stone.

Through the fifty-two-degree lift angle, an angled club tooth on the escape wheel slides across the ruby stone, swinging the pallet fork to kick the balance roller. Then the next tooth drops and locks on the opposite stone, advancing twelve degrees every one hundred and twenty-five milliseconds.
The poised balance wheel and breathing hairspring form a harmonic oscillator beating eight times a second, or 4 hertz, for six hundred and ninety-one thousand two hundred beats every day.

Moving the orange regulator index along the one hundred and eighty millimetre hairspring on the balance wheel tunes daily accuracy: shortening the active spring by eighty-three microns gains twenty seconds a day, and lengthening it by eighty-three microns slows it by twenty seconds a day.
